title: How virtual functions work
objectives: Explain the vtable, object slicing and why a base class needs a virtual destructor.

screens.title: Four bytes from nowhere
screens.prose: Sizes here are for this app's compiler, which is 32-bit WebAssembly: a pointer is 4 bytes. A desktop build has 8-byte pointers.

lines: struct VTick { int px; virtual int level() const; };
sizeof(VTick) is 8 here (16 on a desktop)
params.title: sizes

screens.question: Where do the extra bytes in `VTick` go?

options.text: A hidden pointer to the class's table of functions
A copy of `level`'s code in every object
options.why: You thought each object carries its own code. Code is stored once, in the class, not in each object.
`px` and the pointer are 4 bytes each here, so there is no padding to blame.

options.text: The class name, for run-time type information
options.why: Type information sits in the table, not in each object.

hints.text: Compare the two sizes. What did the `virtual` keyword add?
The extra amount equals one pointer here.
The object points at one table of functions shared by its class.

feedback.correct: A hidden pointer, one per object, to the class's table of functions.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The extra size is exactly one pointer here.

byKey.code: You thought each object carries its own code. Code is stored once, in the class.
byKey.padding: `px` and the pointer are 4 bytes each here, so there is no padding.
byKey.name: Type information sits in the table, not in each object.

explain.text: A class with a virtual function gives every object one hidden pointer, the vptr. It leads to a table of function pointers shared by every object of that class.

screens.title: Follow the call
screens.prose: `p` is a `Payoff*` pointing at a `Call`. The `Put` table is drawn too, as another class's table would be.
screens.question: Tap, in order, what `p->value(110)` visits: the object, its table, the function.

hints.text: Start with the object `p` points at.
The object holds the pointer to a table.
Object, then its own class's table, then the function in slot 0.

feedback.correct: Object, its table, the function: two hops from the object.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows from the object.

byKey.skip: You went from the object straight to the function. There is no such pointer: the call goes through the table.
byKey.put: You took the `Put` table. The object's own vptr leads to its class's table, the `Call` table.

explain.text: The call reads the vptr from the object, goes to that class's table, and calls the function in the slot. The pointer's own type is `Payoff*`, but the table comes from the object.

screens.title: Adding a field
screens.prose: `struct B { int x; virtual void f(); };` is 8 bytes here, with the vptr first. `struct D : B { int y; void f() override; };` adds one `int`.
screens.question: What is `sizeof(D)` here?

hints.text: Start from the 8 bytes of `B`.
D adds one int on top.
8 plus 4. The vptr is not counted twice.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the new field to the size of `B`.

byKey.eight: You counted the two ints and left out the pointer.
byKey.sixteen: That is the desktop answer: its pointer is 8 bytes. Here it is 4.

explain.text: The derived object holds the base part, vptr and `x`, then `y`: 4 + 4 + 4 is 12 bytes here. A desktop gives 16, with an 8-byte pointer.

screens.title: Padding
screens.prose: `struct Quote { virtual double mid() const; double bid, ask; };` A `double` starts on a multiple of 8.
screens.question: Two doubles are 16 bytes. What is `sizeof(Quote)` here?

hints.text: The pointer is 4 bytes here. Where can the first double start?
The next multiple of 8 after 4 is 8.
4 for the pointer, 4 skipped, then 16.

feedback.correct: 24: 4 for the pointer, 4 of padding, 16 for the doubles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A `double` cannot start at byte 4.

byKey.twenty: You added 4 and 16. You left out the padding: a double starts on a multiple of 8, so 4 bytes are skipped.
byKey.sixteen: You counted the two doubles only. The pointer is a real field.

explain.text: The pointer takes bytes 0 to 3, bytes 4 to 7 are padding, and the doubles fill 8 to 23. A desktop also gives 24, for another reason: 8 for the pointer and no padding.

screens.title: Copied into the base
screens.prose: `Payoff` is a concrete base with a virtual `value`. `Call` derives from it. The copy on line 2 holds only a `Payoff`.
screens.question: Which table does `q`'s vptr point to?

options.why: You assumed the copy brings the vptr along. It does not: each constructor sets its own class's table.
`q` is a whole `Payoff` object with its own vptr.

hints.text: Which constructor builds `q`?
It is the `Payoff` copy constructor.
A constructor sets the vptr of the class it belongs to.

feedback.correct: `q` is a `Payoff`, so its vptr leads to `Payoff`'s table.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which class's constructor builds `q`.

byKey.calls: You assumed the copy brings the vptr along. It does not: each constructor sets its own class's table.
byKey.none: `q` is a whole object with its own vptr.

explain.text: This is object slicing: the `Call` part is cut off, and `q.value(110)` runs `Payoff`'s version. That is why cpp-pricing l5 passed `Payoff&`, never `Payoff`.

screens.title: The table by hand
screens.prose: Build what the compiler builds. Each `Payoff` holds a pointer to a table of one function pointer. Write `value_of`, the three functions, the three tables and the three makers.
screens.question: Complete the hand-made virtual call.

tests.setup: Payoff a = make_call(100); Payoff b = make_call(90);
Payoff a = make_call(100); Payoff b = make_put(100);
Payoff c = make_call(100); Payoff p = make_put(100); Payoff d = make_digital(100); const Payoff* book[3] = {&c, &p, &d}; double total = 0.0; for (const Payoff* x : book) total += value_of(x, 105.0);

widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Each call goes through the object's own table; two objects of one kind must share one table.

hints.text: `value_of` has two steps: find the table, call the function in it.
The table is `p->table`, and the function is its `value` field.
`return p->table->value(p, spot);` and each maker passes the address of its own table.

feedback.correct: One table per kind, shared by every object, and the call goes through it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A wrong value means the maker pointed at the wrong table or the function body is off.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Check the table initialisers: `{ call_value }` and the address `&call_table`.

explain.text: The compiler writes the same two steps for `p->value(spot)`: read the table pointer, call the function in the slot. Objects of one kind share one table, so the cost per object is one pointer.

screens.title: Deleting through the base
screens.prose: `Derived` owns a `std::vector<double>`. `Base` has no virtual functions at all.
screens.question: What does the standard say about `delete p`?

options.text: Undefined behaviour: typically `~Derived` never runs and the vector leaks
Defined: only `~Base` runs, and the vector leaks
options.why: You think only `~Base` runs by rule. The rule is that it is undefined, so anything may happen.

options.text: `delete` finds the real type and runs both destructors
options.why: `delete` does not look at the heap block to find the real type.
It compiles; the compiler cannot know the dynamic type here.

hints.text: Which destructor does a call through `Base*` pick when it is not virtual?
The static type is `Base`, and `~Base` is not virtual.
The standard calls this undefined, which is more than a leak.

feedback.correct: Undefined behaviour. In practice `~Derived` is skipped and the vector leaks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the static type of `p` with the type of the object.

byKey.defined: You think only `~Base` runs by rule. The rule is that it is undefined, so anything may happen.
byKey.smart: `delete` does not look at the heap block to find the real type.
byKey.error: It compiles; the compiler cannot know the dynamic type here.

explain.text: A non-virtual destructor is chosen by the pointer's type, and the standard makes `delete` through it undefined. Write `virtual ~Base() = default;`, which costs the 4 bytes of a vptr in each object, as on the first screen.

screens.title: A virtual call in a constructor
screens.prose: `Base`'s constructor sets `who` from a virtual `name()`. `Derived` overrides `name()` to return `"Derived"`.
screens.question: `Derived d;` runs. What does `d.who` hold?

options.why: While `Base` is being built, the object is a `Base`. Its vptr points at `Base`'s table, and `Derived`'s part does not exist yet.
It is well defined: the call goes to `Base::name`.

hints.text: Which constructor runs first, and what is the object's type while it runs?
Line 3 runs inside `Base`'s constructor.
The vptr is set to `Base`'s table at that point.

feedback.correct: `"Base"`: during `Base`'s constructor the object is a `Base`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The base part is built before the derived part exists.

byKey.derived: You expected the real type to win. While `Base` is being built, the object is a `Base`.
byKey.crash: It is well defined: the call goes to `Base::name`.

explain.text: Each constructor sets the vptr to its own class's table before its body runs. So inside `Base()` a virtual call reaches `Base::name`, never the override.

screens.title: What a virtual call does
screens.prose: Order the steps of `p->value(110)` when `value` is virtual and `p` points at a `Call`. One line is not a step.
screens.question: Put the steps in order, and leave the flawed one out.

lines.text: search `Call`'s members by name at run time
lines.why: No search: the slot number is fixed when the class is compiled. A call costs two loads and an indirect jump.

lines.text: index the table at the slot for `value`

hints.text: The table pointer lives in the object.
First the vptr, then the slot, then the call.
Load the vptr, load the slot, jump to it.

feedback.correct: Load the vptr, index the table, call. Two loads and an indirect jump.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The object gives the table, the table gives the function.

byKey.d1: You searched by name. The slot number is fixed when the class is compiled, so there is no search.

explain.text: The slot is a fixed number, so the call is two dependent loads and an indirect jump. Nothing is looked up by name.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.question: A call `p->f()` runs the function of the object's real type when?

options.text: `f` is virtual, and `p` is a pointer or a reference
Always: a pointer always follows the real object
options.why: A non-virtual `f` is chosen by the pointer's type.

options.text: `f` is virtual, even when the object is passed by value
options.why: An object passed by value is a base object: the derived part was sliced off.

feedback.correct: Virtual, and reached through a pointer or reference.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both conditions must hold.

explain.text: A virtual `f` is looked up in the object's own table. A non-virtual `f` is fixed by the pointer's type, and a by-value object is a base object.

screens.title: Ten million lookups
screens.prose: A pricer calls `payoff->value(spot)` 10,000,000 times in a loop. Every payoff in this book is a call.
screens.question: Which change lets the compiler resolve the call at compile time?

options.text: Make the pricer a template on the payoff type, and keep the virtual one for mixed books

options.why: `inline` does not tell the compiler which function a call through a base pointer reaches.
`final` helps only when the compiler can see the exact type.
Calling less changes how often the call runs, not how it is resolved.

hints.text: The lookup exists because the compiler does not know the type.
Make the type known at compile time.
A template instantiates `price<Call>`, so the call is direct and inlinable.

feedback.correct: A template on the payoff type: the call is resolved at compile time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which option tells the compiler the exact type?

byKey.inline: `inline` does not tell the compiler which function a call through a base pointer reaches.
byKey.final: `final` helps only when the compiler can see the exact type.
byKey.fewer: Calling less changes how often the call runs, not how it is resolved.

explain.text: A virtual call costs two dependent loads and an indirect call. It usually stops inlining, because the compiler does not know the target. A template resolves the call at compile time (see cpp l13).

ideas: A class with virtual functions has one table of function pointers. Each object holds a vptr to its class's table, so a `virtual` adds one pointer to every object.
A call through a base pointer loads the vptr, indexes the table and jumps. Slicing copies only the base part, so its vptr is the base's.
Delete through a base pointer only if the destructor is virtual: otherwise it is undefined. During a constructor, virtual calls reach that constructor's class.

formula.name: A virtual call
formula.note: Two loads and an indirect call.

summary.trap: A non-virtual destructor on a base makes `delete p` through a `Base*` undefined, not merely leaky.

quiz.question: What is `sizeof(W)` here?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the hidden pointer.

byKey.four: You counted the `int` only. The hidden pointer is a real field.

options.text: A compile error if nothing in a base is actually overridden

options.why: `override` changes nothing at run time. It is a check.
It only compiles if the base function is already virtual.
The base version is replaced in the table, not hidden by the keyword.

feedback.correct: It catches a typo in the signature.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `override` is a safety check.

explain.text: With `override`, a misspelt name or a missing `const` fails to compile, instead of quietly creating a new function.

options.text: An abstract class: it cannot be built, and each derived class must override `value`
A final class that nothing can derive from
options.why: `final` is a different keyword.
Static means no object. The `= 0` means no body is required here.

options.text: A class that leaks unless it has a destructor
options.why: The `= 0` is about missing bodies, not memory.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A `= 0` function needs no body in the base.

explain.text: A pure virtual function leaves a slot unfilled, so the class cannot be instantiated and acts as an interface.

quiz.prose: A desk keeps `std::vector<Payoff>`, where `Payoff` is a concrete base, and pushes `Call(100)` into it.
quiz.question: What does the vector hold?

options.text: Payoff objects: the Call part is cut off

options.why: The vector stores `Payoff` values, so only that part is copied.
It compiles. The `Call` converts to its base.
A vector of values holds values, not pointers.

feedback.correct: Sliced: only the base part is stored.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The element type is `Payoff`.

explain.text: A vector of base objects copies the base part and drops the rest. Hold `std::unique_ptr<Payoff>` instead.
